findings.message: This fixes only the named case. The decision is not recorded in the same transaction as the write. registry.call(viewer, …) gets no `tx`, so the service commits on its own connection, and close() then runs in the outer transaction that decide() still holds. Two cases are still open. (a) The outer transaction fails or the process dies after registry.call commits. (b) registry.call throws after its commit, for example when the commit ack is lost or the connection resets. In both cases the card goes back to pending and reads as 'nothing changed', so the next confirm runs the write again. Round 5 ended in a stuck 'confirming'; this ends in a duplicate write. permanent() also treats every unrecognised error as retryable, and the new test uses exactly that ambiguous case ('connection reset') as its 'safe to retry' example. A second problem: each confirm now holds one pooled connection, locked, while the service opens a second. With a pool of 1 (common on serverless), or N confirms at once on a pool of N, it deadlocks. Fix: pass `tx` into registry.call so the service write and close() commit together, or make the write idempotent on actionId (store actionId with the created row and look it up before running again). Add a test that kills the outer transaction after registry.call commits, then retries and asserts exactly one row.
findings.scenario: Confirm 'Add X to CON'. create_proposal commits CON-031, then the serverless function times out before the outer transaction commits. The card is pending again. The user clicks 'Add it' and CON-032 is created with the same title: duplicate proposal, two audit rows.

findings.message: Round 6 asked for two variants. Variant 2 (an older numbering such as a round-4 RB-1001) and variant 3 (a spec change ≥1000) were each supposed to assert that both rows survive and the hand-made row is rekeyed. The new table only ever plants a hand-made row on `${P}-002`. The 1001 spec folder syncs onto a free key, so a hand-made `${P}-1001` from round-4 numbering, colliding with spec change 1001, is never tested. That is the one collision the ≥1000 change makes newly reachable. Add a row to the table: hand-made `${P}-1001` exists, spec 1001-big arrives, and the test asserts it was rekeyed to H-series and both rows are present.
findings.scenario: Hand-made P-1001 created under round-4 numbering, then .specclaw/changes/1001-big is added. No test covers the rekey or the skip for this pair.

findings.message: Change numbers can now be longer than 3 digits, but readSpecclaw still sorts them with `a.number.localeCompare(b.number)`. That string sort only works for fixed-width numbers. Sort numerically, e.g. `Number(a.number) - Number(b.number)` or localeCompare with `{ numeric: true }`.
findings.scenario: Changes 200 and 1001 come out in the order 1001, 200.

findings.message: PERMANENT is a hand-kept list of error class names and codes from other packages: core, zod, and delivery's KeyTakenError, which no chat tool can throw. A permanent error that isn't on the list, such as a unique violation (23505) or a renamed error class, is treated as retryable, so the card reopens on every retry forever. Mark errors with a shared property or base class from @amax/core (e.g. `retryable: false`) instead of copying their names.

BusyError means the conversation row is locked, not that this card is being decided. Confirming card B while card A's write runs tells the user 'This is being done right now' for B, which nobody clicked. After 20 polls the card is shown as 'open' even though the state is still unknown. Say 'another action in this chat is running' and report a timed-out poll as unknown, not as open.
